divergencia-kl.d: \( \mathbb D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)=\mathbb E_{y\sim p}[\log p(y)/q(y)] \): how many nats, on average, \( p \) drifts away from \( q \). It is always ≥ 0 and equals 0 only when \( p=q \) (Gibbs' inequality). It is not symmetric.

desigualdade-de-gibbs.d: \( \mathbb D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)\ge0 \), with equality only if \( p=q \). It follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the log. It guarantees that \( \pi^*\propto\pi_{\text{ref}}e^{r/\beta} \) is the unique optimum of KL-regularized RL.

colapso-de-modo.d: When the policy concentrates almost all of its probability on a few responses (or just one) and loses diversity. The KL penalty to the reference exists partly to prevent it.

funcao-de-particao.d: The normalizing constant \( Z(x)=\sum_y\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)e^{r(x,y)/\beta}=\mathbb E_{y\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}}[e^{r(x,y)/\beta}] \): an average weighted by the reference (it equals 1 if \( r\equiv0 \)), computed over every possible response, which makes it intractable. In DPO it cancels out in Bradley–Terry.

inclinacao-exponencial.d: Reweighting a distribution by multiplying each probability by \( e^{r/\beta} \) and renormalizing. It is the form of the optimal policy of KL-regularized RL and reappears in AWR, RWR and ReST-EM.

classe-de-equivalencia.d: Rewards that differ only by a function of the prompt, \( r-r'=f(x) \). They induce the same preferences and the same optimal policy; DPO picks, in each class, the representative with \( Z(x)=1 \).

recompensa-implicita.d: \( \hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} \): the reward that the DPO policy defines. TRL logs it as rewards/chosen and rewards/rejected.

margem-de-log-razoes.d: \( \Delta h=h_\theta(x,y_w)-h_\theta(x,y_l) \), with \( h=\log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}) \). The DPO loss depends only on it: \( -\log\sigma(\beta\Delta h) \).

peso-adaptativo.d: The factor \( \sigma(-\beta\Delta h) \) in the DPO gradient: 0.5 at the start, close to 0 once the pair is well ordered. It focuses learning on the pairs that are still wrong; without it, the model degenerates.

online-dpo.d: At every step, generate two responses with the current policy, ask a judge (an LLM or an RM) which one is better and take a DPO step. It removes the off-policy shift; in OAIF it beat the offline version in ~66% of human evaluations.

dpo-iterativo.d: Rounds of generate → label (RM or judge) → train DPO, where each round uses the policy (and often the reference) from the previous one. Examples: GSHF, Self-Rewarding LMs, IRPO.

llm-juiz.d: Using a language model to compare or score responses in place of humans. It has biases (position, verbosity, self-preference); evaluating in both orders reduces the position bias.

deslocamento-de-verossimilhanca.d: During DPO, the log-prob of the chosen response falls along with that of the rejected one, and the mass goes to other responses, sometimes with the opposite meaning (Razin and colleagues, ICLR 2025).

ches.d: Centered Hidden Embedding Similarity (Razin and colleagues): \( \langle\sum h^+,\sum h^-\rangle-\|\sum h^+\|^2 \) over the hidden states of the two responses. High-CHES pairs tend to cause likelihood displacement; filtering them out mitigates the problem.

win-rate.d: Fraction of comparisons in which the evaluated model beats a baseline model, according to humans or a judge. It depends on the judge (and on its length bias); report it with a confidence interval.

daa.d: Direct Alignment Algorithms: a family of methods that optimize preferences without RL or an explicit RM, such as DPO, IPO and SLiC.
